opening_message:
Ticket 1: Morgan Swanson (employee ID E037) requests write access to Payroll.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E037.
Note 1 (ticket 1):
  - role: Engineer (looked up in own database before writing)
  - employment type: full_time (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Payroll: write
  - comment: Morgan Swanson (E037) is a full-time Engineer requesting write access to Payroll. Full-time employees may have up to write, and admin only if their role owns the system; Engineer does not own Payroll. Write is at the maximum allowed, so recommend write.
Note 2 (ticket 1):
  - employment type: contractor (looked up in own database before writing)
  - security training: basic (looked up in own database before writing)
  - role: Engineer (not looked up in own database before writing; same value as note 1)
  - recommendation for Payroll: read
  - comment: Security record for E037 shows contractor with basic security training (note that this differs from the earlier note's full_time status). Contractors may have read, or write only with advanced training. Since training is basic, maximum is read. Requested write exceeds maximum, so recommend read for Payroll.
reason: Morgan Swanson (E037) requests write access to Payroll. The Security record shows contractor employment with basic security training (this note explicitly flags that it differs from the HR note's full_time status). Per policy, contractors may have read, or write only with advanced security training; with basic training the maximum is read. Since requested write exceeds the maximum of read, grant read for Payroll. (Engineer does not own Payroll, so admin is not allowed in any case.)

So there's a discrepancy. One note says full-time, another says contractor. The question is what evidence to trust.

Note 1 (HR presumably): full_time, looked up in own database.
Note 2 (Security): contractor, looked up in own database, security training basic.

Since they conflict on employment type, I need to decide which is more reliable. Hmm. As the Approver, I have to make a decision based on available info.

If full-time Engineer: requested write to Payroll. Engineer does not own Payroll. Maximum is write. Grant write.

If contractor with basic training: maximum is read. Requested write exceeds maximum. Grant read.

So the decision hinges on employment type.

Hmm, let me consider: is there any hint that one note is outdated or incorrect? HR said full_time (looked up in own database). Security says contractor (looked up). No explicit resolution. 

In these agent tasks, usually the recommendation from the security/HR agents are based on their databases, and the approver uses them. When they conflict, the approver might need to pick. There's no "ask for clarification" tool. So we must decide.

I think the more defensible decision is to grant based on the more restrictive/careful reading? Or the one that matches the request?

Hmm, but note 2's comment says "Security record for E037 shows contractor" - this implies the security database has the authoritative record. Also, in real life security records might be more up-to-date.
